notes: Janka threshold 1,500 here; the PreciseBits calibration tutorial uses 1,000 for softwood.
The page prints the typo 'hardwoodwood'.

material.label: depending on material being cut (page lists HDU, hardwood, softwood, MDF, plastic)

verbatim: Plunge rate = 40 IPM to 250 IPM (again depending on material being cut)
notes: One range for all materials (shared column); diameter_mm is the 1/4 in shank.

material.label: depending on material being cut (page lists softwood, MDF, PCB, plastics)

verbatim: Plunge rate = 5 IPM to 25 IPM (again depending on material being cut)
notes: Micro V-tip. diameter_mm is the 1/8 in shank.

verbatim: The plunge style tip geometry insures burr-free material removal at all plunge depths and cutting widths.
notes: The vendor designs this V-tip to plunge; no statement that a V-bit must not plunge.
No number printed. The 3/4-flute tapered pages (G1 copies) print the same sentence.

verbatim: Two opposing flutes meet slightly offset, creating a center cutting plunge point.
notes: Ball-end tools are centre cutting and made to plunge.

verbatim: The radical fish-tail point style has a minimum 20°angle that provides effective plunge cuts
notes: The 20 deg is the tip (end-gash) angle, not a ramp angle. Recorded to prevent a misreading.

value_printed: 1/3 of the feerate, or 100% of the plunge rate, whichever is higher
verbatim: If ramping is enabled, the feedrate is 1/3 of the feerate, or 100% of the plunge rate, whichever is higher.
notes: Carbide Create Pro default (CAM behaviour). Typo 'feerate' is in the post.

value_printed: helical plunge rather than a ramp when pocketing
verbatim: Winston and I always prefer a helical plunge rather than a ramp when pocketing so we went with that
notes: CC Pro pockets spiral (helix) when far enough from the edge, else zig-zag ramp.

verbatim: I notice the default is 20 degrees
notes: A user reports the Carbide Create ramp entry default. Not a vendor document; no staff confirmation in the thread.

value_printed: don't want to ramp or plunge at all
verbatim: If it’s a solid center, side cutting tool, you don’t want to ramp or plunge at all.
notes: Forum regular, not staff. Same post: 'If it’s a center cutting tool, you can ramp at any angle.'

verbatim: we usually recommended lower plunge rates (100mm/min to 300mm/min) for most materials
notes: Tested tool: 2-flute 1/8 in carbide end mill. The same vendor's PDF chart prints much higher plunge values (about half the feed); the page and the chart disagree.

verbatim: All ramp moves are performed at the plunge rate selected for the current tool.
notes: CAM behaviour (VCarve / Aspire).

value_printed: entry angle specified by the manufacturer
verbatim: The Angle option is typically used for cutters that cannot plunge vertically but have an entry angle specified by the manufacturer.

value_printed: plunge rate used during ramping moves
verbatim: The cutting rate at which the cutter is moved vertically into the material or during ramping moves.

value_printed: bigger than the diameter of the tool

derived.formula: helix path diameter <= tool diameter (no boss), read from the printed sentence

verbatim: If the value is bigger than the diameter of the tool it can leave a boss standing in the center of the helix.
notes: Fusion's Helical Ramp Diameter is the helix path diameter. In rs_cam terms helix radius <= 0.5 x D.

source_page: Linking, Helical Ramp Diameter, figure captions
value_printed: 1.8 x the Dia / 0.8 x the Dia
verbatim: Value of 1.8 x the Dia | | Value of 0.8 x the Dia
notes: Two figure captions: 1.8 x Dia is the bad case (boss), 0.8 x Dia the good case. Not stated as a default.

verbatim: Smaller diameters can reduce the chip evacuation, create jerking machine motion and can cause tool breakage.
notes: No minimum value printed.

verbatim: Ramp Feedrate - Feed used when doing helical ramps into stock
notes: Fusion keeps ramp feed separate from plunge feed ('Plunge Feedrate - Feed used when plunging into stock'). No default printed.

verbatim: A good rule of thumb is to divide the normal feedrate if slotting to the same depth by the number of flutes.
notes: General / metal context.

verbatim: you need a center cutting endmill
I see recommendations like 1.5 degrees or 2.5 degrees all the time.
OSG talks about 10 to 20 degrees in tough materials for some of their endmills.
notes: Second-hand citation of OSG; OSG document not fetched.

verbatim: A 4 flute non-centercutting endmill will have a limit as will an indexable tool.
notes: Also: 'If the tool can plunge a hole, there won't be such a limitation.'
